title: Inverse problems for rule 30 are likely NP-complete

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Inverse problems for rule 30 are likely NP-complete

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Even for the rule 30 cellular automaton, deciding whether initial conditions exist that produce a given outcome after t steps (such as a vertical black stripe of a given height in the center column) is expected to be NP-complete, illustrating that simple instances of NP-complete problems are common.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: my expectation is that asking about possible outcomes of t steps of evolution will already be NP-complete even for the rule 30 cellular automaton

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 12, “The Principle of Computational Equivalence”; section “Undecidability and Intractability” (from p. 753), p. 770. Scope: rule 30 cellular automaton and simple instances of NP-complete problems

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch12-27: needs-new-data, resolvability 0.73

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Once the exact language is fixed, the assertion has a clean proof-based decision criterion. Existing rule data enable experiments, but no finite dataset can substitute for the missing complexity proof.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Specify the rule-30 inverse decision language, encoding of t, target pattern, and admissible initial conditions, then prove membership in NP and either an NP-hardness reduction or a polynomial-time algorithm. The latter would refute NP-completeness unless P=NP.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
A reduction or unexpected algorithm may require new theory.

Several distinct inverse problems are conflated.

Empirical solver scaling cannot establish NP-completeness.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The stripe problem is easy to place in NP, and public simulators can map it at small t. NP-completeness also requires hardness, and that direction remains an open proof obligation for rule 30. Proofs that some other cellular automata have NP-complete preimage problems bear on the remark that simple instances occur, and they leave the rule 30 expectation unresolved.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Given t, decide whether some initial condition makes rule 30 produce a center-column black stripe of a stated height after t steps. A polynomial reduction from a known NP-complete problem would confirm the expectation, and a polynomial algorithm would refute it. Guess-and-simulate already places the problem in NP.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Membership in NP is immediate; NP-hardness of this rule 30 problem is open.

NP-complete preimage problems for other cellular automata do not transfer to rule 30.

Empirical hardness at small t is compatible with a polynomial algorithm.
